alignments.note: Rule 9: subject and lexical verb, headed on the verb.

The supplied indefinite is the indefinite pronoun's own helper and *certain* carries the lexeme, as at 9:10 and 9:36 and as the corpus reads *a certain* on tis in seventeen units. That the Greek writes the indefinite after its noun here changes nothing; ACT.10.1 gives the *a* to the noun instead and remains defensible.
The noun stands bare, its determiner having gone to the indefinite.
The participle is rendered as a finite relative clause; the supplied relativizer and auxiliary are its rule 7 and 9 helpers.
Rule 36: the ASV's *kept his bed* absorbs the preposition into the predicate, so English realizes it nowhere.
Anarthrous noun; the supplied possessive is a rule 7 helper on the noun.
Rule 36: the ASV writes *eight years* with no preposition, so this ex is realized nowhere.

The ASV recasts the relative clause as a causal one; the relative is what the supplied *for he* answers to (rule 40's principle that a subordinating element takes whatever introduces its English clause), as at 9:35 and 9:39. Marking *for* added under rule 86 remains defensible.

review_notes: Only the tina / anthropon edge changed: tina now takes *a certain* headed on *certain*, and anthropon takes a bare *man*. This also removes a discontinuous noun unit that jumped over *certain*.

Rule 58's determiner-to-the-noun clause is scoped to a Greek adjective with an expressed noun; an indefinite tis is a determiner in its own right, which is why the corpus lets it carry the whole English determiner expression.

The rest of the verse holds, including the two rule 36 unrepresented prepositions (epi absorbed into *kept his bed*, ex written with no preposition in *eight years*) and the supplied causal *for* taken with the relative hos.
